title: Right to Know CLG & Environmental Protection Agency
text:
Decision
Right to Know CLG & Environmental Protection Agency
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-142453-C8K0S2
Published on 22 June 2026
Chronology
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the EPA was entitled to rely on article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations
22 June 2026
Chronology
1. In January 2022, the appellant submitted two (2) AIE requests seeking access to certain data from the water abstraction register maintained by the EPA in accordance with
S.I. No. 261/2018 - European Union (Water Policy) (Abstractions Registration) Regulations 2018
(“the 2018 Regulations”). In a combined original decision dated 11 February 2022, the EPA identified and part-granted access to an abstraction register excel sheet. Following a request for internal review, on 8 March 2022, the EPA affirmed its original decision; which was appealed to this Office in
OCE-120518-X2W6N8
. In the decision on that appeal, dated 1 June 2023, the Commissioner annulled the decision of the EPA concerning certain withheld information and directed it to undertake a fresh decision-making process in respect of that information.
2. On 17 August 2023, the EPA issued a fresh decision, informing the appellant that it had decided to part-grant the information, and further, that it would publish the abstraction register on its website no later than 25 August 2023, subject to redactions for “personal data that could identify an individual person”, citing article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations and Article 6 of the 2018 Regulations which it noted states that the EPA “may share details entered onto the register in relation to an abstraction, with the exception of personal details, with such other person as it considers necessary for the discharge of its statutory functions, or to enable any other public body to satisfactorily discharge its statutory functions”. This decision was also subject to an internal review process under article 11 of the AIE Regulations; being upheld in full in the internal review outcome dated 15 September 2023.
3. The appellant submitted a further appeal to this Office on 19 September 2023 as follows: “Note this is the [second] time this refusal by EPA has been appealed. In this case, we're not appealing the redaction of the entire Abstractions Register, just the redaction of the agricultural related abstractions.”
4. In submissions to this Office dated 14 November 2023, the EPA stated: “In the interests of making as much information as possible on the abstractions register publicly available in August [2023], the EPA took a cautious approach when redacting names to avoid releasing personal information in breach of our GDPR responsibilities.” It went on to outline that it had subsequently reviewed the published register and had decided where it is clear the abstractor is a company e.g., “Limited”, “Ltd”, “Partnership”, “Company” etc., that the next iteration of the published register, due in December 2023, would publish previously redacted information relating to that record, as the EPA no longer considered this to be “personal information”. However, it indicated that other redactions would remain as, in the EPA’s view, “in accordance with the GDPR Regulations, article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations, Section 37 of the FOI Act 2014 and Article 6 of [the 2018 Regulations], it is not in the public interest to release [other] personal information, as to do so would lead to the identity of natural persons.”
5. On 30 January 2025, this Office asked the EPA to confirm, given the passage of time, whether it continued to rely on article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations in the matter of this appeal. In response dated 6 March 2025, the EPA stated that it “continues to rely on article 8(a)(i) as outlined in [its] submission [dated 14 November 2023]”. It also referred to new abstraction legislation introduced in August 2024 and advised that “the EPA has been developing an abstraction licensing portal, which includes the abstractions register, and this will be a live portal similar to other EPA licensing regimes… due to go live at the end of February 2025”.
6. On 8 July 2025, this Office contacted the appellant to confirm if it wished to continue with the appeal given the introduction of the EPA’s new abstraction licensing portal. The Investigator noted her preliminary view, that the new live abstraction register appeared to contain certain information which had previously been refused by the EPA under article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations, including ‘Organisation Name’, ‘Site Location’ and ‘Scheme/Licence Name’ for agricultural related abstractions. In response dated 5 September 2025, the appellant confirmed that it wished to continue, for reasons including its view that “EPA and other public bodies continue to redact agri environmental mapping data”, and also its view that “the online portal does not appear to match the AIE request”. In this regard, the appellant provided a number of site location examples, exported from the abstraction register, which it noted were marked as ‘Redacted’.
7. In February 2026, this Office contacted the EPA, including to ascertain what exact information from the water abstraction register excel sheet, within scope of the Commissioner’s previous decision dated 1 June 2023, continues to be withheld by the EPA on the basis of article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations. In response dated 26 February 2026, the EPA informed this Office that “following the enactment of new legislation… and the development of an abstractions licensing regime and online portal, the EPA will no longer be relying on article 8(a)(i), i.e. the EPA does not withhold any previously withheld information relevant to this case i.e. non-drinking water abstractions.”
8. In May 2026, the Investigator wrote to the appellant setting out the EPA’s updated position. The investigator also addressed the site location examples provided by the appellant in its previous correspondence dated 5 September 2025. She noted, following examination, that these examples represented industrial or drinking water related abstractions, whereas the scope of appellant’s appeal in this case was limited to agricultural related abstractions. The Investigator set out her view that all information within the scope of this appeal is now publicly available via the EPA’s online portal and again asked the appellant to confirm whether it would like to continue with the current appeal. In response dated 22 May 2026, the appellant confirmed that it would still like to continue to decision.
9. I am directed by the Commissioner for Environmental Information to carry out a review of this appeal. I have now completed my review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In so doing, I have had regard to the fresh decision-making process undertaken by the EPA, correspondence between this Office and both the EPA and the appellant in this matter, and I have also reviewed the relevant information. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (‘the Minister’s Guidance’);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (‘the Aarhus Convention’); and
• The Aarhus Convention – An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
10. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
11. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, the role of this Office is to review the EPA’s internal review decision (dated 15 September 2023) and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, the Commissioner will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
12. This review is concerned with whether the EPA was entitled to rely on article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations to withhold the information specified at point 67 of the Commissioner’s decision in OCE-120518-X2W6N8 dated 1 June 2023, and solely concerning agricultural related abstractions as specified in the appellant’s statement of appeal dated 19 September 2023.
Analysis and Findings
13. The 2018 Regulations, that established a water abstraction register, were formally revoked on 28 August 2024, with enactment of the
Water Environment (Abstractions and Associated Impoundments) Act 2022
(“the Principal Act”) and
S.I. No. 419/2024 - Water Environment (Abstractions and Associated Impoundments) Regulations 2024
(“the 2024 Regulations”), which introduced a new registration, licensing and control regime for water abstractions and associated impoundments. Section 63(2) of the 2024 Regulations, in line with Section 10(7) of the Principal Act states that the EPA “may publish any of the information contained in the register as it considers appropriate on a website maintained by it or in such other manner as it considers appropriate.” The current abstraction register is publicly available
here
.
14. During the course of this Office’s investigation, it became apparent that all information which could be considered within scope of this appeal is now available from a continuously updated and publicly available database. On this basis, the Investigator attempted to find an informal resolution to preclude the issuing of a formal binding decision. However, this was not possible.
15. A review by this Office is considered to be de novo, which means that it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of this decision. This approach has been endorsed by the decision of the High Court in M50 Skip Hire Recycling Limited v the Commissioner for Environmental Information
[2020] IEHC 430. As such, there is no requirement for this Office to review the substantive matter of whether the EPA was entitled to refuse the information at issue, as the EPA has essentially reversed its decisions and is no longer relying on its original grounds for refusal.
16. However, it is also the case that the EPA’s fresh decision-making did not outline any consideration of the public interest balancing test obliged under article 10(3) and 10(4) of the AIE Regulations regarding the information concerned, nor did it detail the adverse impact of disclosure of this information. The balancing test is a mandatory component of the AIE regime, where the scheme of the AIE Regulations, and of the AIE Directive upon which the Regulations are based, makes it clear that there is an inherent presumption in favour of release of environmental information. As the Minister’s Guidance at para. 13.4 outlines: “It is important to note that this "public interest" test applies to all applications for information irrespective of whether any provision of Article 8 or Article 9 may apply in relation to a particular application. In other words, even where the information would normally be comprehended by a provision for protecting information under Article 8, the information should be made available if, in the opinion of the public authority, the public interest is best served by doing so.”
17. Article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations provides that a public authority shall not make available environmental information where disclosure of the information would adversely affect the confidentiality of personal information relating to a natural person who has not consented to the disclosure of the information, and where that confidentiality is otherwise protected by law.
18. The Commissioner’s previous decision dated 1 June 2023 in this matter outlined the requirements in order to engage article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations (see para. 53.). It was also set out at para. 58. of that decision that: “The GDPR and the Data Protection Acts do not provide for a blanket prohibition on the disclosure of personal data as part of an AIE request. They do so by providing that refusal is only permissible in circumstances where disclosure would adversely affect the confidentiality of personal information.” In more recent decisions by this Office (available at
www.ocei.ie
), the Commissioner has considered the relevance of engaging an analysis of the EU GDPR legislative regime, finding that it harmoniously interacts with AIE in the context of article 8(a)(i). When examining the applicability of this provision to an AIE request, the public authority should first consider the lawful basis of the processing of personal data set out in article 6 of the GDPR. The public interest test, obligated by article 6(1) of GDPR and 10(3) of the AIE Regulations are considered as one in the same, that is, just one test is carried out, to fulfil the requirements of both regimes. The public interest test considers each request on an individual basis and weighs the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal, including consideration of the data rights of the data subjects, any potential adverse impact of release and, the general interest served by release of environmental information in the context of the AIE regime and its objectives.
19. In processing future requests, I would encourage the EPA to be mindful of its obligations, to either provide the requester with the environmental information requested or a reasoned decision as to why refusal is appropriate, having regard to all of the requirements of the AIE Regulations.
Decision
20. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, on behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental information, I hereby annul the EPA’s decision to rely on article 8(a)(i) of the AIE Regulations. As the EPA is no longer relying on article 8(a)(i) to withhold any information within scope of this appeal, I make no further direction.
Appeal to the High Court
21. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information
